brief.head: A one-way door
brief.text: Amit Varma op­poses the death penalty: the state is “a fum­bling beast” that has ex­e­cuted in­no­cent men. Ajay Shah cited a pol­icy prin­ci­ple: do things that you can undo. {085-C04}

brief.head: Monkey business
brief.text: Some dic­ta­tors turn out well by dumb luck, Ajay Shah said, just as some mon­keys pick good port­fo­lios. That does not make mon­keys good at port­fo­lio choice. {085-C05}

brief.head: Whiners and doers
brief.text: Asked at a party to com­plete “There are two kinds of peo­ple in the world”, Amit Varma said: the whin­ers and the doers. Pick friends who are doers. {085-C09}

brief.head: Atoms on loan
brief.text: Legacy is van­ity, Amit Varma said. Ajay Shah agreed: “Life is the whim of a few tril­lion atoms to be you for a while.” {085-C14}

brief.head: Hold that thought
brief.text: Amit Varma judges people’s think­ing by how often they in­ter­rupt. Men, he said, in­ter­rupt women on con­fer­ence pan­els all the time, often with­out re­al­is­ing it. {085-C26}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah give the world three grades
lead.head: Rated, berated and complicated

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 85

body: The crew threw words at the hosts, and the hosts threw back one of three ver­dicts: un­der­rated, over­rated or com­pli­cated. Amit Varma had added the third to a fa­mil­iar in­ter­net game, for things that look un­der­rated from one angle and over­rated from an­other. {#complicated}
The re­sult was the show’s long­est episode so far, two hours and fif­teen min­utes on ev­ery­thing from cities and cin­ema to Elon Musk, mar­riage, Maggi and death.
One word was ruled out be­fore the first throw. Freedom, the hosts agreed, is un­der­rated, and they speak about it so much al­ready.

The open­ing ver­dicts came eas­ily. Cities are un­der­rated, Varma said, be­cause “peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs”: den­sity brings di­verse peo­ple to­gether and lets them spe­cialise in deeper ways. {085-C01}
Ajay Shah called vil­lages “a hot­bed of ig­no­rance, su­per­sti­tion, and un­free­dom”. Moving to the city, he said, “is the be­gin­ning of free­dom”.
Curiosity, Shah said, is treated as some­thing cute and ju­ve­nile. “I want to say that ex­tended ju­ve­nil­ity is the essence of good­ness and great­ness.” {085-C02}
## Agree to dis­agree
After the death sen­tence, Varma no­ticed a prob­lem. “So far we are agree­ing on ev­ery­thing. This is a bit wor­ry­ing. Can we learn to dis­agree?” {#agreeing}

Bob Dylan obliged. Shah called him a bad singer whose songs should be left to oth­ers. Varma and the crew sang *Lay Lady Lay* in a full nasal twang, to show that some songs only Dylan can sing. {085-J03}

Then came Elon Musk. Varma called him a pi­o­neer­ing thinker whose bets on elec­tric cars, bat­ter­ies and space de­fied con­ven­tional think­ing. Shah saw sur­vivor­ship bias: “There are 16,384 Elon Musks. And out of dumb luck, we are ven­er­at­ing one.” {085-C06}

The sharpest fight was over flat-earth the­ory, which both called non­sense. Varma de­fended hereti­cal think­ing as the way hu­man­ity pro­gresses. Shah wanted a lot less so­cial media and a lot more rev­er­ence for knowl­edge. {085-C08}

They met part­way, agree­ing that an or­di­nary per­son can de­fault to the con­ven­tional view while a gen­uine heretic should still speak up. On so­cial media they did not: a net pos­i­tive for Varma, who built his ca­reer on it, and a net neg­a­tive for Shah.
## Theories of liv­ing

The mid­dle of the episode turned per­sonal. Varma of­fered his “Bengali the­ory” of hap­pi­ness: at any mo­ment, a small act, a song, a call to a friend, some bacon, can make the next in­stant hap­pier. {085-C11}
Shah’s an­swer to Varma’s ode to Bengali melan­choly was three words long. “Ice cream is bet­ter.” {085-J12}

They split again over pills. Varma takes modafinil on record­ing days, as “a tool and not a crutch”. Shah prefers no props at all, not even caf­feine, be­cause dis­ci­pline builds char­ac­ter. {085-C21}
Even tal­ent was marked down. What we call a child’s tal­ent, Shah said, is usu­ally “dumb luck and ac­ci­dents”: praise for some­thing, more prac­tice, then skill. {085-C28}

The last word was death. Shah, wor­ried about the longevity ex­plo­sion, called it un­der­rated. Varma said no­body re­ally rates it at all, be­cause ev­ery­body is in de­nial, and left the sub­ject for an­other episode so that they could end on a happy note. {#happynote}
His phi­los­o­phy of hap­pi­ness, he said, is sim­ple: “You can be happy when­ever you want.”

second.label: Fathers and sons
second.head: The hug that came late
second.deck: Amit Varma on seeing parents as people, and counting the visits left

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his father’s one awkward hug

body: Amit Varma’s fa­ther, in his last years in Chandigarh, seemed to be try­ing to reach out. Once, as Varma was get­ting into his Uber after a visit, his fa­ther opened his arms. They had never re­ally hugged. {085-S06}
Varma gave him a very awk­ward hug. He had once recorded his fa­ther talk­ing about his life for a cou­ple of hours, but it was a one-off, and a lot re­mained un­said.

Most peo­ple, Varma said, see their par­ents only in the job de­scrip­tion of fa­ther or mother. His ex­er­cise for read­ers: cal­cu­late how many more times you will see them. The num­ber will be so small that you should call them right after the show. {#visits}

quote.text: And I went and I gave him a very awk­ward hug and I re­spected the mo­ment. But it was just one mo­ment.

third.head: Next stop, Kanyakumari

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the walk that need not end

body: Ajay Shah is cur­rently at about twenty trail days a year, roughly ten in the Sahyadris and ten in the Himalayas. With fewer con­straints, he said, it would only be more.
His one story of hik­ing: he and Ayush Patnaik were walk­ing a north-south route through the Sahyadris in Maharashtra. By day eight or nine, they looked at each other.
“We could just keep going till Kanyakumari,” Shah said. “It’s like why would we ever stop?” {085-S03} Ten to thirty kilo­me­tres a day would get them there.

Amit Varma, who does not go on hikes, de­clined to say a word about it. But he re­called the day be­fore the shoot, when Shah was asked whom he would take on a last hike. Shah’s an­swer, “Amit, will you come?”, made ev­ery­one tear up a bit. {085-S04}

box.title: The first name on the list
box.text: Frédéric Bastiat was the first name the crew threw, and Amit Varma rated him un­der­rated: a writer who put com­plex ideas sim­ply with­out dumb­ing them down. His essay *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen* named Varma’s pod­cast. {085-R02}

sections.label: Cities and curiosity
sections.head: Rabbit holes welcome
sections.caption: why people are brains, not stomachs
body: The open­ing ver­dicts were unan­i­mous. Cities, Amit Varma said, bring di­verse peo­ple to­gether, which en­larges your world­view and your ex­po­sure to art, cul­ture and ideas. Larger eco­nomic net­works let peo­ple spe­cialise. People crib about traf­fic, but they keep mov­ing to cities. “They vote with their feet.” {085-C01}
Ajay Shah said vil­lages are a hot­bed of ig­no­rance and un­free­dom, and Varma re­called B.R. Ambedkar’s phrase, “dens of ig­no­rance and vice”.

Curiosity got the same grade. A friend com­plained to Varma that he had spent three hours in a rab­bit hole that had noth­ing to do with his life. Varma’s reply: “Fantastic. That’s what you should do.” {#rabbithole}
## Know thy­self

Evolution, Shah said, ap­plies far be­yond bi­ol­ogy: to ji­hadist groups in Iraq, to busi­ness mod­els, to com­puter soft­ware. Varma added that you can only know your­self through evo­lu­tion­ary bi­ol­ogy and psy­chol­ogy, be­cause we are not blank slates. But an ought does not fol­low from an is, and our in­stincts often con­tra­dict each other. {085-C03}
Varma rec­om­mended Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate*, and said, ad­mit­ting the hy­per­bole, that he di­vides his life into be­fore and after read­ing it. {085-R05}

~ The hu­man­i­ties were un­der­rated too, though Varma had noth­ing but con­tempt for hu­man­i­ties de­part­ments. {085-C13} Shah ex­plained STEM’s pres­tige: it is easy to teach and to test. Prove Pythagoras’ the­o­rem in an exam hall, and you can be thrown Apollonius’ the­o­rem next.

sections.label: Luck and failure
sections.head: Moonshots or lucky dice?
sections.caption: Elon Musk and survivorship bias
body: Elon Musk pro­duced the sec­ond dis­agree­ment of the day. Ajay Shah said there is a large el­e­ment of luck in the mak­ing of every rich per­son, after which great man syn­drome leads them to opine on ev­ery­thing. He rec­om­mended the hosts’ own episode *A Country Is Not a Company* to Mr Musk. {085-R09}
Amit Varma called Musk a pi­o­neer­ing thinker, whose bets on elec­tric cars, bat­ter­ies and space went against con­ven­tional think­ing.
Shah replied that a rough idea that the RBI needs re­form is very dif­fer­ent from ac­tu­ally doing it. {085-C06}
Few peo­ple even at­tempt such au­da­cious bets, Varma coun­tered, and even if only one in a hun­dred sur­vives, “we need all those hun­dred”. {#audacious}
## Wish them fail­ure

Failure, Varma said, is un­der­rated. Anything good in him comes from hav­ing failed all his life, which stripped away his hubris and en­ti­tle­ment and turned him from a whiner into a doer. {085-C07}
Shah added that mass cul­ture wor­ships bil­lion­aires, and re­called an old Marwari cul­ture in which a man’s worth is mea­sured by the num­ber of failed busi­nesses he has run.
~ Talent, by con­trast, was over­rated. Varma re­called an athlete’s def­i­ni­tion of it: going run­ning at 5 am, hun­gover, with a cold and the next event six months away, in the rain. {085-S10}

quote.text: The best thing I can wish for for a young per­son is I wish you fail­ure.

art.caption: Amit Varma on Elon Musk and survivorship bias

sections.label: The big fight
sections.head: Flat earth, open minds
sections.caption: heretics and reverence for knowledge
body: Flat-earth the­ory, both hosts agreed, is com­plete non­sense. What fol­lows from that was their sharpest dis­agree­ment. {#hogwash}

Amit Varma still found some­thing to de­fend. Heliocentrism was once heresy, he said, and so was ques­tion­ing the con­sen­sus that sugar is fine and fat is the prob­lem. American guide­lines en­shrined that con­sen­sus in 1977, and the obe­sity epi­demic began. {#sugar}
Gregor Mendel, a com­plete out­sider, was recog­nised only after his death; Ignaz Semmelweis was ig­nored for decades. Thinking hereti­cal thoughts, Varma ar­gued, is how hu­man­ity pro­gresses.
## Who gets a say

Ajay Shah was “a lit­tle more sta­tus quo”. Experts de­fine what is open for de­bate: in­ter­mit­tent fast­ing is, a flat earth is not. A teenager de­cid­ing on Reddit whether a COVID vac­cine works, he said, is the mod­ern post-truth world.
“The cri­sis of the mod­ern world is an as­sault on knowl­edge,” Shah said. {085-C08}
They partly con­verged. An or­di­nary per­son, Varma con­ceded, can de­fault to the con­ven­tional view, while a heretic should put their ideas out there.

~ On so­cial media they parted again. Shah thinks it a net neg­a­tive. Varma ac­cepts Jonathan Haidt’s re­search on teenage girls, but said a cu­rated feed lets you hear “the best minds in the world think­ing aloud every day”. {085-C17}

quote.text: It is im­por­tant to think hereti­cal thoughts for hu­man­ity to progress.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on heretics and reverence for knowledge

portraits.credit: József Borsos / Albert Doctor, public domain

sections.label: Less is freer
sections.head: Own less, gossip less
sections.caption: why frugality buys freedom
body: Ajay Shah opened with a bor­rowed line: “Freedom’s just an­other word for noth­ing left to lose.” The lower your fixed com­mit­ments, he said, the freer you are. {085-C10}

Amit Varma agreed that clear­ing out the inessen­tial frees space in your head. He could live out of a suit­case, he said, be­cause the real value is in the cloud and in his re­la­tion­ships. But he would not be dog­matic: books, good food and com­fort­able travel are fine if you can af­ford them. Just don’t buy pri­vate jets.
Shah, for his part, mar­velled at the mir­a­cles they take for granted. His XKDR Forum rents a GPU for eight dol­lars an hour, a ca­pa­bil­ity he called unimag­in­able. {085-C16}
## Mind your hours
Gossip, Varma said, is the most toxic thing in the world. “I would never speak bad things about any of you be­hind your back, but I have to your face very often.” {085-J06}

Shah’s friend Josh Felman, an older fig­ure who com­manded re­spect, had a cure. Whenever talk turned to who was sleep­ing with whom, he would put his hands down and say, “It’s not im­por­tant.” {085-S02}
~ Little minds dis­cuss peo­ple, medium minds dis­cuss news, great minds dis­cuss ideas, Shah said. Watch your hours: the rest is petty bick­er­ing. {085-J28}

quote.text: The lower the op­er­a­tional lever­age of your life, the more you get free­dom. So fru­gal­ity buys you free­dom. The price of free­dom is fru­gal­ity.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on why frugality buys freedom

sections.label: Love and kin
sections.head: Unbundling the marriage
sections.caption: marriage as a bundled package
body: Marriage, both hosts said, is com­pli­cated. Amit Varma cred­ited Ajay Shah with the frame: mar­riage is a pack­age of love, sex, ro­mance, com­pan­ion­ship, par­ent­hood and friend­ship. Few peo­ple un­bun­dle it in their heads, so when one part falls apart, ev­ery­thing seems to. {085-C15}

Shah called it an in­sti­tu­tion of the agri­cul­tural world of re­li­gion and pa­tri­archy, out of touch with a post-industrial age that is closer to the hunter-gatherer one. The 20th cen­tury, he added, put an ex­ces­sive bur­den on one per­son to be your ev­ery­thing.

Varma said both of them were tak­ing a priv­i­leged male view. For most women in India, he said, mar­riage is closer to im­pris­on­ment. Chinmay Tumbe’s *India Moving* shows that most in­ter­nal mi­gra­tion in India hap­pens when women marry and move to their husband’s place. {085-R14}
## The con­sent ar­gu­ment

Varma once wrote a tongue-in-cheek col­umn ar­gu­ing that hav­ing chil­dren is im­moral: a child can­not con­sent to being born, will feel pain and will die. Then he shrugged. We do many sin­ful things, he said, like the white lies that sus­tain friend­ships, so go ahead. {085-C12}

~ Shah rated par­ent­hood un­der­rated. Parent-child jour­neys are among the great ones, he said, once you strip away re­source-intensive, he­li­copter, per­for­ma­tive and com­pet­i­tive par­ent­ing.

quote.text: I only wish it had been us, but I’m happy for your hap­pi­ness.
quote.who: Warren Zevon, as quoted by Amit Varma

art.caption: Amit Varma on marriage as a bundled package

quote.text: Happiness is not some­thing you ex­pe­ri­ence, it is some­thing you re­mem­ber. As the years go by and as I have be­come older, life is ac­tu­ally a col­lec­tion of peak ex­pe­ri­ences.

p3.title: Stories between verdicts
p3.deck: Four tales the hosts told along the way

stories.kicker: Amit Varma, out of retirement, on a game with new rules
stories.head: First principles, first in Asia
body: Playing for the coun­try was one of the words thrown at the hosts. Ajay Shah rated it over­rated. Amit Varma called it com­pli­cated, and de­clared an in­ter­est: he has played for India.
Varma was a pro­fes­sional poker player for five years, until 2015. Then a friend who owned the Haryana Hawks, a team in an IPL-style league, brought him out of re­tire­ment.

The game was match poker, which changes the rules so that the usual heuris­tics no longer apply. You had to think from first prin­ci­ples and sort out the new game. “And I did, and no one else did,” Varma said. {085-S09}
The Hawks won twice. Then Varma played for India, and the team won the Asian cham­pi­onship.

At the world cham­pi­onship in Greece, India got slaugh­tered. Three team­mates could not get visas, and the re­place­ments had to be taught a shared strat­egy on the fly. It was, Varma said, a night­mare.
He had a sim­i­lar run in chess vari­ants on chess.com, Atomic and Fog of War, where he was briefly num­ber one until he got bored. The joy, he said, was in fig­ur­ing out first prin­ci­ples.
His de­fence of play­ing for the coun­try, partly tongue in cheek, was nar­row: in some sports, such as Olympic events, the na­tional team is the only stage there is.
~ Shah had made his own case first. Gukesh won the world cham­pi­onship in chess, he said. “You didn’t, I didn’t.” {085-C22}
stories.why: When a game is new, in­her­ited heuris­tics stop work­ing and who­ever rea­sons from first prin­ci­ples takes the edge. Varma did it twice, in match poker and in chess vari­ants on chess.com. {085-S09}
stories.postscript: Varma rec­om­mends the show’s poker episode for more on his five years as a pro­fes­sional.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on playing poker for India

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a father, a son and a supply of Marvel
stories.head: A ration of Marvel
body: In early-1980s Chandigarh, Amit Varma re­called, for­eign comics were nearly im­pos­si­ble to find be­yond the likes of Phantom and Indrajal. His fa­ther found a sup­plier in Delhi and brought back Marvel and DC comics from his trips.
He handed them over three at a time, and said three was all he had. When Varma got re­ally bored, three more ap­peared.

Varma knew there were more. “So now game the­ory comes into play,” he said. {085-S05} He schemed to get them sooner, his fa­ther fig­ured out he was play­ing the game, and it be­came an early game of poker.

~ Through those comics he fell for the Marvel uni­verse of Stan Lee and his col­lab­o­ra­tors, whose char­ac­ters were shades of grey. The Marvel Cinematic Universe, he said, is a cyn­i­cal com­mer­cial ex­ploita­tion of the fran­chise.
stories.why: Varma calls it a good mem­ory of his fa­ther: two peo­ple play­ing game the­ory with each other, each know­ing the other knew. It also ex­plains his split ver­dict on Marvel, un­der­rated on the page and over­rated on screen.
stories.postscript: Shah asked whether the films could be made by an LLM. Varma: “Iron Man 38 can of course be made by LLM.” {085-J10}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his father’s comics ration

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an observation made over tea
stories.head: A scandal of sameness
body: Over tea, while record­ing an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, a friend of Amit Varma’s, “a dis­tin­guished gen­tle­man who also hap­pens to be gay”, said that two young celebri­ties had done Botox. One of them was about 20.
Varma was shocked. That was noth­ing, the friend said: they had boob jobs too.

Then he leaned for­ward. “Amit, I want you to go out there and I want you to look at the breasts of young women today. Look closely. They are all the same.” In his time, he said, there was va­ri­ety and di­ver­sity. It was a scan­dal. {085-S08}

~ Varma says he did not fol­low the in­struc­tions. His own stance is to be com­fort­able in your own body, with ex­cep­tions for health and for re­pair after ac­ci­dents, and to treat any­one who judges your looks as toxic.
stories.why: Behind the de­light­ful rant was a real point: cos­metic pro­ce­dures sand away human va­ri­ety. Ajay Shah linked it to fash­ion. These are su­per­fi­cial props, he said, and the life­long jour­ney is one of build­ing char­ac­ter.
stories.postscript: Shah’s sound­track: the Eagles, whose high-livers “took all the right pills”. {085-J27}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on a friend’s rant about sameness

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a happy accident in his kitchen
stories.head: Fluke in the frying pan
body: Amit Varma once ate one meal a day, be­tween five and seven in the evening, and was ten kilos lighter. He cooked three-course meals for him­self.
One day he mar­i­nated prawns in gochugaru, a Korean spice, with olive oil and gin, then cooked them in olive oil with lots of but­ter and bird’s-eye chilli.
His mind was blown for two rea­sons. “One rea­son was that this is the best prawn I have ever eaten. And the sec­ond rea­son was I made it.” {085-S07}

~ He called it a happy ac­ci­dent, or “the Elon Musk of my food”: sur­vivor­ship bias, one in a mil­lion that hap­pened to be good. “Though you said it about Elon Musk,” he told Ajay Shah, “I don’t.” {085-J16}
stories.why: Culinary ex­per­i­men­ta­tion is un­der­rated, Varma said. He hates pineap­ple on pizza but de­fends the right to try it, and likes chowmein dosa, be­cause all food evolved from some­thing else. Ajay Shah added that this is how we keep in­vent­ing stuff.

quiz.q: Which writer’s essay gave Amit Varma’s podcast, The Seen and the Unseen, its name?
quiz.a: Frédéric Bastiat, with *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen*.

quiz.q: How many Elon Musks did Ajay Shah say are out there rolling the dice?
quiz.a: 16,384, and out of dumb luck we ven­er­ate one of them.

quiz.q: How did Amit Varma complete the party game “There are two kinds of people”?
quiz.a: The whin­ers and the doers: a vi­cious cycle against a vir­tu­ous one.

quiz.q: Where did Ajay Shah and Ayush Patnaik realise they could simply keep walking to?
quiz.a: All the way to Kanyakumari, from a north-south route in the Sahyadris.

quiz.q: What happens to Amit Varma’s chess.com rating when he is on modafinil or keto?
quiz.a: It goes up by about a hun­dred points, and drops back af­ter­wards.

quiz.q: Why does Warsaw mean more to Ajay Shah than Prague does?
quiz.a: He has spent years read­ing about Poland, and knows lit­tle about Prague.

Limits on our cir­cles: the five, the fif­teen, the hun­dred and fifty.
Recording that cap­tures ev­ery­thing, so sound never clips: audio’s RAW.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 85. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Frédéric Bastiat (Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0); Gregor Mendel (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Ignaz Semmelweis (József Borsos / Albert Doctor, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0).

shelf.title: The collected writings of Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: The writ­ings of ‘the man who re­ally turned me on to freedom’, as Amit puts it: Bastiat put com­plex eco­nomic ideas into sim­ple lan­guage with­out dumb­ing them down, and gives you a frame­work for see­ing the world.

shelf.title: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s bro­ken-window para­ble, which teaches you to look past a policy’s vis­i­ble ef­fect to its un­seen costs and in­tro­duced op­por­tu­nity cost decades be­fore the term ex­isted.

shelf.title: The Law
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s mid-19th-century mas­ter­piece on the re­la­tion­ship be­tween the state and so­ci­ety, which Amit says car­ries wis­dom in every para­graph and is a strik­ingly mod­ern lens on India.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson
shelf.creator: Henry Hazlitt
shelf.why: Hazlitt’s 1946 ‘col­lec­tion of light bulbs’ that uses the ba­sics of scarcity and in­cen­tives to clear up fal­la­cies about price con­trols, tar­iffs, in­fla­tion and gov­ern­ment spend­ing, teach­ing you to ask what the money would have done if left with con­sumers.

shelf.title: The Blank Slate
shelf.creator: Steven Pinker
shelf.why: Amit’s gate­way into nat­u­ral se­lec­tion and evo­lu­tion­ary psy­chol­ogy: Pinker ex­am­ines human na­ture and so­ci­ety through our evo­lu­tion­ary hard­wiring.

shelf.title: The Paper Menagerie
shelf.creator: Ken Liu
shelf.why: Ken Liu’s col­lec­tion, whose title story Amit calls a mas­ter­piece of ‘de­clut­tered language’ (noth­ing in it doesn’t be­long) that will leave you weep­ing; he sends it to his writ­ing stu­dents, and the rest moved him to tears at in­di­vid­ual sen­tences.

shelf.title: Malayalam and Marathi cinema
shelf.why: With the main­stream crum­bling and the means of pro­duc­tion avail­able to ev­ery­one, the ex­cit­ing ac­tion is in world and indie cin­ema, not stan­dard com­mer­cial fare.

shelf.title: Bob Dylan’s own recordings (e.g. Lay Lady Lay)
shelf.creator: Bob Dylan
shelf.why: Dylan’s voice is au­then­tic to his music, and some songs only he can sing; Amit and the crew sang Lay Lady Lay to prove it needs his nasal twang.

shelf.title: A Country Is Not a Company (Everything is Everything episode)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why busi­ness in­tu­itions don’t carry over to pub­lic pol­icy: pol­i­cy­mak­ing is a com­pletely dif­fer­ent and hard-won body of knowl­edge, and for­get­ting that is the trap be­hind many calls for in­dus­trial pol­icy.

shelf.title: The Outlaws (Everything is Everything episode)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Stories of mav­er­icks such as Semmelweis, Mendel and Darwin who were ig­nored by the es­tab­lish­ment and vin­di­cated late, some­times at the cost of lives.

shelf.title: Jonathan Haidt’s books on social media
shelf.creator: Jonathan Haidt
shelf.why: They lay out the re­search on the dam­age so­cial media has done to so­ci­ety, es­pe­cially to the men­tal health of young peo­ple and teenage girls.

shelf.title: Jonathan Haidt’s episode on Brave New World
shelf.creator: Vasant Dhar
shelf.why: Haidt ex­plains the stud­ies link­ing so­cial media to teenage de­pres­sion, es­pe­cially among girls.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: India Moving
shelf.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
shelf.why: Amit calls it one of the great books of the last ten years.

shelf.title: El Amor de Mi Vida
shelf.creator: Warren Zevon
shelf.why: Lines like ‘I only wish it had been us, but I’m happy for your happiness’ show true love as want­ing the other per­son to be happy, not own­ing them.

shelf.title: The Wind
shelf.creator: Warren Zevon
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great album.

shelf.title: Rode Wireless PRO (32-bit float audio)
shelf.creator: Rode
shelf.why: Microphones that record 32-bit float audio, which Amit calls mirac­u­lous: like RAW for pho­to­graphs, it cap­tures ev­ery­thing, so sound never clips and lev­els can be fixed af­ter­wards.

shelf.title: Salil Chowdhury’s music for Anand
shelf.creator: Salil Chowdhury
shelf.why: It is his sound­track for a per­mit­ted half-hour of lux­u­ri­at­ing in melan­choly.

shelf.title: Amit’s episode with Abby Philips (The Liver Doc) on The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long de­fence of sci­en­tific medicine from liver doc­tor Abby Philips, on the ten­sion be­tween doing right by pa­tients and giv­ing them what they want.

shelf.title: Amit’s COVID-era episode with Lancelot Pinto on The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Dr Lancelot Pinto, one of the rare doc­tors who reads pa­pers daily, on med­i­cal prac­tice and how overtreat­ment driven by pa­tient de­mand cost lives dur­ing COVID.

shelf.title: The Cats
shelf.creator: Ann Iverson
shelf.why: It is a de­light­ful por­trait of crea­tures who find glory in a de­hy­drated pea and find them­selves ‘so re­mark­able all the day long’.

shelf.title: Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat
shelf.creator: Samin Nosrat
shelf.why: It teaches you to think in four el­e­ments, how they act and com­bine.

shelf.title: A Poetry Handbook
shelf.creator: Mary Oliver
shelf.why: It cov­ers the me­chan­ics of lan­guage, not just of po­etry.

shelf.title: The Broken Script
shelf.creator: Swapna Liddle
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite his­tory books: Delhi from 1803 to 1857, when Persian col­lapsed, print and news­pa­pers boomed and po­etry was pop­u­lar cul­ture, until it all ended in 1857.

shelf.title: Why We Sleep
shelf.creator: Matthew Walker
shelf.why: The book that taught Amit how un­der­rated sleep is: with­out it you can’t be your best self, sleep-deprived driv­ers are more dan­ger­ous than drunk ones, and night owls, roughly 30% of peo­ple, sim­ply run on a dif­fer­ent rhythm.

shelf.title: Matthew Walker’s episode on the Huberman Lab podcast
shelf.creator: Andrew Huberman
shelf.why: In it, Walker ex­plains the im­por­tance of sleep.

shelf.title: Inverting the Pyramid
shelf.creator: Jonathan Wilson
shelf.why: It is a great book on foot­ball tac­tics.

shelf.title: The Blue Book, The Yellow Book and The Green Book
shelf.creator: Amitava Kumar
shelf.why: The books are jour­nals com­bin­ing writ­ing and draw­ing, and they model the daily writ­ing habit Amit says will shape you into a richer, deeper per­son.

shelf.title: The poker episode of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: What Amit’s five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player taught him about life: most of what hap­pens is luck, so don’t let suc­cess go to your head or fail­ure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

shelf.title: The hiking episode of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay on his pas­sion for hik­ing, from the Goecha La trek be­neath Kanchenjunga to why the worst ac­ci­dents hap­pen when you think you’re al­most home.

laughs.text: Amit, rhap­so­dis­ing about cities: ‘There is noth­ing like going to a mall at ten AM as it is open­ing. The smell of fresh com­merce in the morn­ing.’

Amit on Indian menswear: ‘There are no slim fit men in India... They’re com­plete freak­ing out­liers.’ Then he thanked H&M for stock­ing every fit: ‘H&M, if you’re watch­ing this, ei­ther H or M, hats off to you.’
Amit de­fend­ing white lies: ‘every time I ask you, Ajay, am I look­ing fat? You say no, no, no. Now you’re clearly lying, but it is for a good rea­son, and I ap­pre­ci­ate that.’
Amit on navel gaz­ing: if you sit by the sea­side look­ing out to sea ‘and there are ships, it’s also naval gaz­ing.’ Ajay: ‘Yes, that is very funny. But more sub­stan­tively...’

Bob Dylan’s line ‘He not busy being born is busy dying’, quoted by Amit on why adults who stop being cu­ri­ous es­sen­tially die. Later Ajay quoted an­other Dylan line on fail­ure: ‘There’s no suc­cess like fail­ure, and failure’s no suc­cess at all.’
